# Taiwan Gray Zone Monitor — Full Description

> Taiwan Gray Zone Monitor is an open-source intelligence (OSINT) dashboard
> that monitors maritime "gray zone" activity in the waters around Taiwan in
> near real time. It integrates AIS vessel-position data, SAR satellite
> dark-vessel detections, Global Fishing Watch data, and the CSIS "Signals in
> the Swarm" threat methodology to surface and risk-rank suspicious behavior.

Live site: https://s0914712.github.io/taiwan-grayzone-monitor/
Source code: https://github.com/s0914712/taiwan-grayzone-monitor
License: MIT
Contact: s0914712@gmail.com
Languages: Traditional Chinese (zh-TW) and English

## What "gray zone" means here

Gray-zone maritime activity refers to coercive or ambiguous actions that stay
below the threshold of open conflict — for example fishing-fleet aggregation,
AIS manipulation, suspicious loitering near submarine cables, and covert
ship-to-ship transfers. These are hard to attribute and easy to deny, which is
why open-source cross-referencing of AIS and satellite data is useful.

## Monitoring area

Approximately 20–28°N and 112–128°E, covering the Taiwan Strait, the waters
east of Taiwan, and parts of the South and East China Seas.

## Data sources

1. Taiwan Port Bureau AIS feed — vessel positions, names, types, timestamps.
2. Global Fishing Watch (GFW) — SAR (synthetic aperture radar) satellite
   detections, used to find "dark" vessels that appear on radar but broadcast
   no matching AIS signal.
3. CSIS "Signals in the Swarm" report — methodology for cable-proximity,
   zigzag, going-dark, and identity-manipulation detection.
4. UN sanctions vessel list — for sanctions matching.
5. ITU MARS ship-station registry — for verifying ship name, IMO, and call sign.
6. Submarine cable route geometry — for proximity and loitering analysis.

## What the project detects

- Dark vessels: SAR detections with no corresponding AIS broadcast.
- Suspicious vessels: scored on an 8-criterion engine (see Methodology).
- Ship-to-ship (STS) transfers: vessels rendezvousing at close range (<~10 m
  separation) for a sustained period — a possible covert-transfer signature.
- AIS identity changes: name, MMSI, or type changes within a rolling window.
- Chinese fishing-fleet aggregation and Chinese government / special-interest
  vessels (coast guard, maritime safety, rescue, research) by name keyword.
- Submarine-cable threats: vessels loitering or behaving anomalously near cables.

## Threat-scoring methodology (summary)

Each known vessel is classified by a per-vessel risk score built from eight
criteria: (1) cable proximity and loitering, (2) zigzag course pattern,
(3) time spent near the 200 m depth contour, (4) AIS anomalies (name/type
changes, going dark, identity events), (5) non-top-10 flag state, (6) UN
sanctions match, (7) AIS spoofing (impossible physics, box pattern, circle
pattern), and (8) ITU MARS registry mismatch, plus ship-to-ship transfer
involvement. Behavioral scores are weighted by vessel type (e.g. cargo and
tanker ×1.0, fishing ×0.2). Risk levels: critical (≥12), high (≥8, flagged as
suspicious), medium (≥5), normal (<5). Full details are on the Methodology page.

## Update frequency

- AIS vessel positions: every 2 hours
- SAR / Global Fishing Watch dark-vessel analysis: every 12 hours
- CSIS suspicious-vessel analysis: every 12 hours
- Ship-to-ship transfer detection: every 2 hours
- AIS identity-change detection: every 2 hours

The pipeline runs on GitHub Actions and publishes to a static GitHub Pages site
with no server-side backend. Timestamps are ISO 8601 (UTC).

## Methodology limitations and responsible use

- AIS positions can be incomplete due to relay delay, coverage gaps, or a
  vessel intentionally switching off its transponder.
- A SAR detection means a radar-visible target; it does not by itself prove
  illegal activity.
- A high suspicious score is a risk ranking to assist human analysts — it is
  not a legal determination of wrongdoing or intent.
- Ship-to-ship detections may include lawful operations such as pair trawling,
  resupply, or waiting at anchor outside a port.
- The project is an analytical aid, not a substitute for professional
  intelligence assessment.

## Citation guidance

When citing this project, attribute it as "Taiwan Gray Zone Monitor"
(台灣灰色地帶與海底電纜監測), an open-source OSINT dashboard, and link to
https://s0914712.github.io/taiwan-grayzone-monitor/ . Please note that threat
scores are risk rankings, not legal findings, and that AIS and SAR data have
the limitations described above.

## Disclaimer

This project is provided for research and educational purposes under the MIT
License. It aggregates publicly available data and does not assert that any
named vessel has engaged in illegal activity. Conclusions drawn from this data
are the responsibility of the user.
